big: Meena holds a bond that pays 7% a year. Then new bonds start paying 8%. Her bond has not changed at all, yet the market now values it less. This is why debt funds can dip.

lines: Why did my debt fund go down? Debt funds are supposed to be safe.
A fund values its bonds every day at market prices. Let us see what one rate rise does to one bond.
But the bond still pays the same coupon!

alt: Bars of the price fall for a 10-year and a 2-year bond when yields rise by 1%
caps: Two bonds, both 7% coupon, both priced at ₹1,000. Then market yields rise from 7% to 8%.
New bonds now pay ₹80. Nobody pays full price for an old bond that pays ₹70.
The 10-year bond falls to about ₹933, a loss of ₹67. The 2-year bond slips only to about ₹982.
Same rate rise, but the longer bond fell almost four times as much.

intro: Face value ₹1,000, coupon ₹70 a year, ten years left. Each price is the value of all future payments at that yield.
note: Rates up, price down. Rates down, price up. The prices are computed by discounting every payment at the yield.

h: Hold on, and the price comes home
alt: Three lines of a ten-year bond price: flat, falling after a jump to 8% and falling after a jump to 9%, all returning to 100
caps: One 10-year bond with a 7% coupon, priced at ₹100. These paths are made up.
In year 1 market yields jump to 8% or to 9%, and the price drops at once.
Each year the bond has less time left, so the price drifts back up towards ₹100.
Hold to maturity and you collect every coupon plus ₹100 back. The dip was only on paper.
A fund must mark its bonds daily, so its NAV shows the dip.

q: Meena owns a 7% ₹1,000 bond with ten years left. New 10-year bonds are now issued at 8%. A buyer offers her about ₹933 for hers. Why would anyone pay less than face value?
opts: Second-hand bonds always sell at a 7% discount to face value
The issuer has cut the coupon on old bonds after the rate rise
A new bond pays ₹80, so the older ₹70 bond has to be cheaper
The buyer wants a profit before the issuer repays face value
why: There is no fixed discount. The price depends on the yield buyers want and the time left, here ₹933 for ten years.
Coupons on existing bonds never change. What changed is the market yield, which lowers the price of the old bond.
A new bond pays ₹80 on ₹1,000. To match that, the old ₹70 bond has to sell at a price that makes its yield about 8%.
A buyer's profit does come from price and coupon, but the discount exists because of the new 8% yield, not a wish for profit.

q: A client's long-duration debt fund shows -2.1% for the month after the RBI raised rates. She says debt funds are safe and wants to know if the fund has defaulted. What is the fair explanation?
opts: The fund has missed coupon payments, and she should plan to exit
The fund's bonds were repriced for higher yields, and the coupons are still being earned
The fund house has charged a one-time fee that month for the rate rise
The NAV only moves when the fund sells a bond, so some sale must have gone wrong
why: A missed coupon is a default, which is a credit event. Nothing in the story says that. A rate rise explains the dip.
The NAV marks every bond to the market each day. Prices fell on the rate rise, while the fund still earns its coupons.
No such fee exists. The cost of a fund is the expense ratio, spread across each day's NAV, not a lump sum for a rate move.
NAV is marked to market daily, whether or not the fund sells anything. A fall in bond prices is enough to dip it.

q: Both a 2-year and a 10-year bond pay a 7% coupon at ₹1,000. Yields rise from 7% to 8%. About how much does each fall in price?
opts: Both fall by about ₹10, one point of yield being ₹10 of price
Both fall by about ₹70, which is the full coupon on ₹1,000
About ₹67 for the 2-year and about ₹18 for the 10-year bond
About ₹18 for the 2-year and about ₹67 for the 10-year bond
why: Price moves are not the same for every bond. The longer one is hit far harder by the same rate rise.
₹70 is one year of coupon, not the loss in price. Neither bond falls that much from a 1% yield rise.
This reverses the rule. The short bond has less time to suffer the lower coupon, so it falls less, not more.
The 2-year drops to about ₹982 and the 10-year to about ₹933. Longer maturity, bigger swing.

q: Rohan's 10-year 7% bond is down on paper after a rate rise. The issuer is sound and he does not need the money for nine more years. What happens to the price if he simply holds?
opts: It drifts back towards ₹1,000 as maturity nears
It stays at the lower price for as long as rates stay high
It falls further each year, as less time is left before maturity
It returns to ₹1,000 the day the RBI stops raising rates
why: At maturity the issuer repays face value, so the price is pulled towards ₹1,000 and he is paid coupons all along.
With each year the bond has less time left, so the price is pulled back towards face value even if yields stay high.
Time works the other way. With fewer years left the discount shrinks, so the price rises towards face value.
A pause in rate rises does not reset prices. Price depends on yields and time left, and neither jumps back on a pause.

pts: Rates up, prices down. Rates down, prices up.
The longer the bond, the bigger the price swing for the same rate change.
A fund marks bonds daily, so the swing shows in NAV. Held to maturity, the bond still pays face value.
